exam: What are the five steps of the clinical audit cycle and why is each essential? — Explain each step, linking it to measurable improvement.
A child with severe pneumonia dies despite antibiotics. How would you design an audit to prevent this? — Identify a relevant standard, data sources, and likely system gaps.
Why is a clinical audit not considered research, and what ethical implications does this have? — Discuss purpose, consent, and data use.
In a low‑resource ward, pulse oximetry is unavailable. How would you audit oxygen‑therapy compliance? — Use clinical signs as proxy and describe limitations.

Your audit shows 40 % of neonates do not receive first‑dose antibiotics within 1 hour. List three root‑cause categories and one practical change for each. — System, staff, patient factors with specific actions.
How can the Hawthorne effect distort audit results and how would you mitigate it? — Explain the effect and propose blinded data collection or prolonged observation.
During re‑audit, performance improves but mortality remains unchanged. What does this tell you? — Discuss the need to choose outcome‑linked standards.
Compare clinical audit with incident reporting in terms of scope and impact on patient safety. — Highlight differences in proactive vs reactive approaches.
ai.title: Paediatric Clinical Audit
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Clinical audit is a systematic review of paediatric care against agreed standards, aiming to improve practice. It involves measuring current performance, identifying gaps, implementing change, and re‑auditing. In low‑resource settings the cycle must be pragmatic and use locally available data.

b: Standard: clear, measurable criteria (e.g., % children receiving WHO‑recommended malaria treatment within 1 hour).
Data source: patient notes, drug registers, ward registers, or simple observation sheets.
sections.p: A clinical audit compares actual paediatric care with explicit, evidence‑based standards. It is not a research study; it measures routine practice to identify improvement opportunities.

b: Minor gap: <10 % deviation, low‑risk outcome.
Moderate gap: 10‑30 % deviation, potential morbidity.
Major gap: >30 % deviation or linked to mortality/serious harm.
sections.p: Audit findings are graded by the size of the performance gap and the clinical impact of the missed standard.

b: System: drug stock‑outs, lack of guidelines, inadequate staffing.
Staff: insufficient training, unclear roles, high turnover.
Patient: late presentation, cultural beliefs, transport barriers.
sections.p: Reasons for poor performance fall into three categories: system, staff, and patient factors.

b: Trigger: unexpected mortality, high readmission rate, or external accreditation request.
sections.p: Audit is usually initiated after a sentinel event (e.g., a child death from preventable sepsis) or as part of routine quality‑improvement meetings.
Data collection tools answer specific quality questions.

t.b: Does the child receive the correct drug, dose, and timing? → Identifies prescribing errors or stock‑outs.
What proportion of admitted children have a documented vital‑signs chart? → Highlights gaps in monitoring.
Do caregivers understand discharge instructions? → Assesses health‑education effectiveness.

t.a: If a test is unavailable (e.g., pulse oximeter)
t.b: Use clinical signs (cyanosis, respiratory rate) to approximate oxygenation status.

b: No audit of emergency triage → delayed treatment of severe malaria or sepsis.
Missing audit of immunisation records → outbreaks of vaccine‑preventable disease.
sections.p: Failure to audit high‑risk processes can perpetuate preventable deaths.

b: Choose a locally relevant topic first (e.g., timely antibiotics for neonatal sepsis).
Set standards from WHO or national guidelines; keep them measurable.
Analyse data with simple charts; involve the whole team in root‑cause analysis.
Implement change: training, checklists, supply‑chain fixes.
Re‑audit after 3‑6 months to confirm improvement.
sections.p: The audit cycle consists of five steps: (1) choose topic, (2) set standards, (3) collect data, (4) implement change, (5) re‑audit.

b: Monthly audit briefings at ward meetings.
Public display of key indicators (e.g., % children with fever receiving antimalarial within 1 hour).
sections.p: Sustain gains by embedding audit results into routine supervision, creating a visual dashboard, and linking performance to staff appraisal.

b: Research aims to generate new knowledge; audit measures existing practice.
Quality‑assurance checks compliance after the fact; audit is cyclical and improvement‑focused.
sections.p: Clinical audit is distinct from research, quality‑assurance surveys, and incident reporting.

b: Hawthorne effect: documentation improves temporarily during audit period.
Incomplete records can hide missed care; cross‑check with pharmacy logs.
sections.p: Self‑reported data may over‑estimate performance because staff know they are being observed.
